title: APIs and Data Exchange
eyebrow: System boundaries · How software asks other software for work or data
summary: Follow one application asking an invoice service for work, then expand that simple conversation into the real rules an API needs: operations, inputs, responses, errors, security, retries, pagination, webhooks, GraphQL, events, and safe change over time.
sectionTitles: 1. Start with a software conversation, not the word API
2. HTTP gives a web API standard request and response semantics
3. Both sides need the same understanding of the data shape
4. Errors need machine-readable structure and useful human meaning
5. Proving identity and granting permission are different decisions
6. Real APIs must behave predictably when data is large or networks fail
7. Choose the communication style from who needs to talk, when, and how
8. An API is not dependable if changing it silently breaks its consumers

An API is not dependable if changing it silently breaks its consumers API An Application Programming Interface: a defined boundary through which software can request capabilities or data from another component. Contract The testable agreement describing operations, inputs, outcomes, errors, security/operational behavior, and change rules at a software boundary. Schema A formal or documented definition of a data shape and its constraints. Authentication The process of establishing who or what a caller is. Authorization The decision about whether an established caller may perform a particular action on a particular resource under current policy. Cursor pagination Pagination that continues from an opaque position in an ordered result set instead of relying only on numbered pages. Backoff A retry strategy that waits between attempts, commonly increasing the delay for later attempts. Jitter Random or varied delay added to retry timing so many clients are less likely to retry simultaneously. Idempotency A defined property where repeating an equivalent operation does not create additional unintended effects beyond the contract's intended result. Webhook An HTTP callback sent by a provider to a registered consumer endpoint when a defined event occurs. Deprecation A notice that an interface is still available but is planned to be replaced or removed, accompanied by a migration path and timeline.

title: Git and GitHub
eyebrow: Delivery workflow · Remember, compare, share, review, and recover
summary: Learn Git by following a project through real state changes: edit files, choose what belongs in the next saved snapshot, commit it, branch safely, share it with another repository, review it on GitHub, automate checks, and recover from mistakes.
sectionTitles: 1. Git solves the problem of remembering project states
2. An edit moves from working files to the next snapshot to committed history
3. Commits connect into history; branches are names that point into that history
4. Branches let work diverge; merge and rebase change how histories come together
5. A remote is another Git repository, not a magical cloud copy of your folder
6. GitHub adds review, permissions, policy, and collaboration around Git history
7. GitHub Actions turns repository events into repeatable jobs
8. Recover by identifying where the unwanted change exists

Recover by identifying where the unwanted change exists Repository Git's stored project history and references, commonly used with a checked-out working tree. Working tree The checked-out project files on disk that you directly edit. Index · staging area Git's proposed content for the next commit. Commit A recorded project snapshot with metadata and one or more parent links connecting it to history. Branch A movable Git reference that usually points at the newest commit in one line of work. HEAD Git's reference identifying what is currently checked out; commonly it points to the current branch. Remote A named configuration for communicating with another Git repository. Remote-tracking reference A local reference such as origin/main that records the remote branch state known from the last fetch. Pull request A GitHub collaboration object for reviewing and integrating proposed changes between branches. Workflow GitHub Actions automation defined in YAML and triggered by configured repository events. Reflog A local log of recent updates to references and HEAD that can help locate previously known commits during recovery.

title: How the Web Works
eyebrow: Foundation · One address-bar request from start to finish
summary: Follow what actually happens after you enter a web address: the browser finds the destination, creates a protected connection, asks for resources, receives a response, and turns the result into a page.
aliases: what happens when I open a website
sectionTitles: 1. Pressing Enter starts a round trip
2. The web address tells the browser where to begin
3. The browser turns the site name into a network destination
4. The browser creates a path for the conversation and protects HTTPS traffic
5. HTTP says what the browser wants and what the server decided
6. The browser turns returned resources into the page you see
7. Debug by finding the earliest stage that failed

URL A structured resource address that can contain a scheme, host, port, path, query, and fragment. Domain name A human-readable name in the DNS naming system, such as example.com; it can appear as the host part of a URL. DNS The distributed Domain Name System that provides records for names, including records that map a host name to IP addresses. IP address An Internet Protocol address used by networks to identify and route toward a network interface or destination. Transport The communication layer that carries application data with defined delivery behavior, such as TCP or QUIC in common web stacks. TLS Transport Layer Security, which authenticates peers and protects data in transit for HTTPS. HTTP The web application protocol that defines request and response semantics. Header A named HTTP field that carries information used to understand or control request/response handling. DOM The Document Object Model: the browser's object representation of the document that scripts and browser APIs can inspect and change. Rendering The browser work that converts document, style, script, media, and state into the visual interface.

title: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript
eyebrow: Frontend foundation · Meaning, appearance, and behavior
summary: Learn the three core browser languages by building one small page: HTML gives content meaning and structure, CSS controls presentation and layout, and JavaScript adds behavior when the page needs to react or change.
sectionTitles: 1. Start with one page and separate its three jobs
2. HTML tells the browser what the content is
3. CSS turns rules into presentation
4. JavaScript reacts when the page needs behavior or changing state
5. Build the useful baseline first, then enhance it
6. Responsive design means the content keeps working as its context changes
7. Put the model together with one disclosure component

Put the model together with one disclosure component HTML HyperText Markup Language, the web markup language used to describe document content, structure, and native controls. Semantic HTML Choosing HTML elements because their defined meaning and behavior match the content or task. CSS Cascading Style Sheets, the language used to describe presentation and layout for structured documents such as HTML. Cascade The CSS conflict-resolution process that decides which applicable declarations win when multiple rules set the same property. JavaScript A programming language commonly used in browsers to react to events, coordinate state, call APIs, and change application behavior. DOM The Document Object Model, the browser's object representation of the document that APIs and scripts can inspect and change. Event A notification that something happened, such as a click, input, submit, timer, or network-related result. State Information an application needs to remember so it can determine its current behavior or interface. Browser API A capability supplied by the browser environment to code, such as the DOM, Fetch, History, Storage, media, or timers. Progressive enhancement Starting with a functional baseline and adding richer supported capabilities without making the baseline unusable.

title: The 7 Types of Databases
eyebrow: Data systems · Match the database to the questions your software must answer
summary: Learn seven practical database families by starting with familiar data questions—orders, nested content, sessions, relationships, measurements, text search, and similarity—then continue into schemas, transactions, indexes, consistency, specialized stores, and production trade-offs.
sectionTitles: 1. Start with the questions your software must answer
2. Relational databases are strong when facts relate and rules span records
3. Document databases keep data that belongs together in one nested record
4. Key–value databases optimize the shortest path to a known item
5. Graph databases make relationships part of the primary model
6. Time-series, search, and vector stores optimize three specialized retrieval problems
7. Add another database only when its benefit pays for another source of failure
8. Turn the seven families into a repeatable selection process

Turn the seven families into a repeatable selection process Access pattern A recurring way an application reads or writes data, such as lookup by id, join by relationship, time-window aggregation, text ranking, or vector similarity search. Invariant A condition the system must preserve as data changes, such as uniqueness or a business rule that forbids an invalid state. Constraint A rule enforced by the database to reject data states that violate the declared model. Index An additional data structure designed to speed selected retrieval patterns at the cost of storage and work when data changes. Transaction A unit of database work whose operations follow defined commit/rollback, isolation, and durability guarantees. Aggregate A group of related data treated as one meaningful loading or consistency boundary in a domain model. Traversal Following graph relationships from one node to connected nodes, potentially across several hops. Inverted index A search data structure that maps analyzed terms toward the documents or fields containing them so text matching can be efficient. Embedding A numeric vector produced by a model to represent features of an item such as text or an image for downstream comparison or retrieval. Projection A derived representation of authoritative data shaped for a particular read, search, similarity, analysis, or caching need. Polyglot persistence An architecture that intentionally uses multiple data-storage technologies because different workloads benefit from different models.
